nameStory: The sharksucker gets its name from its amazing ability to literally stick to sharks and other large marine animals! It has a special sucker disc on top of its head that works like a powerful vacuum, allowing it to hitch rides on its much larger hosts. This incredible adaptation turns the sharksucker into the ocean's ultimate hitchhiker.
description: The sharksucker is a sleek, torpedo-shaped fish that's built for life as an ocean traveler. This remarkable fish has evolved a flat, ridged sucker disc on the top of its head that it uses to attach to sharks, rays, turtles, and even boats. Sharksuckers are typically brownish-gray with darker stripes running along their streamlined bodies, and they can grow up to about 3 feet long. While extremely rare in New England waters, they occasionally show up attached to larger marine animals during warmer months.

idTips.label: Sucker Disc
idTips.description: The unmistakable flat, oval disc on top of the head with ridged slats that feel like a ribbed rubber mat - no other New England fish has anything like this attachment organ

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely streamlined and torpedo-shaped with a flattened head, built for reducing drag while attached to fast-moving hosts

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Brownish-gray overall with dark horizontal stripes along the sides and a lighter belly, giving it a subtle camouflaged appearance

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long, continuous dorsal and anal fins that extend along most of the body's length, with a distinctive forked tail fin

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Can reach up to 3 feet in length, making it one of the larger remora species, with a firm, muscular body

habitat: Sharksuckers are open ocean wanderers that are extremely rare visitors to New England waters. When they do appear, it's typically in deeper offshore waters during the warmest summer months, usually attached to large sharks, rays, or sea turtles that have traveled north with warm Gulf Stream currents. They might occasionally be spotted near the surface in areas where their hosts are feeding or traveling.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be seen, as water temperatures are still too cold for this warm-water species to venture into New England waters.
seasonality.summer: The only season when sharksuckers might possibly appear in New England, typically attached to large pelagic sharks or rays in offshore waters during the warmest weeks.
seasonality.fall: Any individuals present would likely move south with their hosts as water temperatures begin to drop in late summer and early fall.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters, having migrated south to warmer Atlantic waters with their hosts.

funFact: A sharksucker can create such strong suction with its head disc that researchers have measured attachment forces strong enough to support the fish's entire body weight - it's literally designed to never let go even when its host is swimming at full speed through turbulent water!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded observation in New England, there's little chance of confusion - no other fish in our waters has the distinctive sucker disc on its head. If you see a fish with this feature, you've found something truly extraordinary!
contextualKnowledge: While called a 'sharksucker,' this fish doesn't actually suck blood or harm its host - it's a harmless hitchhiker that feeds on scraps from its host's meals and small parasites. The relationship is generally beneficial for both species, making the sharksucker nature's cleanup crew.
compareHints: As the only remora species recorded in New England waters, the sharksucker stands alone in its family here. Other remora species found in warmer Atlantic waters are generally smaller and have different sucker disc shapes, but all share the distinctive hitchhiking lifestyle. The sharksucker is among the largest and most streamlined of all remoras.
